taxonomy.note: Accepted by current Kew/POWO; native range Texas to Mexico. Older literature may list it as Commelina anomala, Commelinantia anomala, or Tradescantia anomala.

evidence: BONAP/NAPA provides a county map for Tinantia anomala and Kew/POWO accepts Texas in the native range.
Travis County — UT Plant Resources Center's Travis County Commelinaceae herbarium index includes Tinantia anomala.
Williamson County — UT Plant Resources Center provides a detailed county treatment for Tinantia anomala.
Val Verde County — the Amistad National Recreation Area vascular flora documents Tinantia anomala on rocky slopes, flats, ledges, and intermittent drainages.
target_zone_range.guardrail: Tinantia anomala is an annual and may colonize garden settings. County proof uses herbarium/floristic evidence, not horticultural occurrences.

morphology.look_here_first: Look at the inflorescence bract and upper leaves. Tinantia anomala lacks a closed dayflower spathe pocket: the terminal one-sided cyme sits above a broad leaflike bract that is mostly open/flat, while the upper leaves often have rounded to cordate clasping bases. Then confirm two large blue-lavender petals, one small white petal, and six fertile stamens with conspicuous filament hairs.
diagnostic_traits: annual, tufted to several-stemmed herb, commonly up to about 60–80 cm
stems cylindrical rather than strongly flattened, often pinkish-purple near exposed nodes
basal/lower leaves narrower and often petiolate; upper cauline leaves broader and sessile
upper leaf bases often rounded to cordate-clasping around the stem
terminal one-sided cyme with several flowers
large subtending bract is leaflike and mostly flat/open rather than forming a closed fused spathe pocket
flowers about 2–2.7 cm across with two broad blue-to-lavender petals and a much smaller white lower petal
six stamens are fertile and heteromorphic; several filaments have conspicuous violet/yellow-tipped beadlike hairs
persistent boat-shaped sepals conceal the developing capsule

confusers.separator: Commelina erecta has the unmistakable folded/fused green spathe pocket enclosing buds and fruit. Tinantia instead has an open leaflike bract subtending an exposed terminal cyme; its upper leaves also more strongly clasp the stem.
Tradescantia spiderworts usually have three comparably showy petals. Tinantia has two large blue/lavender petals plus one much smaller white petal, and its one-sided cyme/bract architecture differs.

Tropical spiderwort/dayflower is an invasive Commelina with a true spathe and often reddish hairs on leaf sheaths. Tinantia lacks that Commelina spathe pocket and carries its flowers on an open terminal cyme.

diagnostic_roles: flower face showing two large petals and small white petal
photo_verification.provenance_note: The best visual lesson is an inflorescence-side image showing the open leaflike bract, clasping upper leaf and exposed cyme together.
